title: Strings, interpolation and formatting
body: A `string` is an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units. Methods such as `ToUpper`, `Replace` and `Trim` return new strings and never modify the original. Because of immutability, building a long string by repeated `+=` in a loop copies repeatedly; `System.Text.StringBuilder` appends into a growable buffer instead.

Interpolated strings start with `$` and embed expressions in braces: `$"{name} is {age}"`. A format specifier follows a colon (`{price:F2}` for two decimals, `{n:N0}` for digit grouping, `{x:X}` for hex) and an alignment follows a comma (`{word,-8}` pads to 8 characters, left-aligned). Formatting uses the current culture unless you pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`; the guide's checks run with invariant culture.

Escape sequences such as `\n` and `\t` work in regular literals. A verbatim literal `@"C:\temp"` treats backslashes literally. Raw string literals use three or more double quotes and can span lines without escaping quotes; the indentation of the closing quotes is removed from every line. Combine `$` with a raw literal for templated text such as JSON.

`Length` counts UTF-16 code units, not user-perceived characters: an emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane uses two. Index with `s[0]` for a char, and use ranges such as `s[1..4]` (start inclusive, end exclusive) or `s[^3..]` for the last three characters.

Compare strings deliberately. `==` compares content ordinally for strings. For user-facing or case-insensitive comparisons pass a `StringComparison`, for example `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`. Check culture, case and length semantics whenever text crosses a boundary such as a file, a URL or a user.

challenge: Use a StringBuilder to build the string 0,1,2,3,4 with commas between numbers and no trailing comma, then print it and its Length.
question: What does `s.ToUpper()` do to the string stored in `s`?
correct: Nothing; it returns a new upper-case string
reasoning: Strings are immutable. Assign the result (s = s.ToUpper()) if you want the variable to refer to the new value.
